lesson.title: Länder I: Deutschland, Frankreich, England, Spanien, Italien
lesson.subtitle: five country names — the ones English kept, the ones it renamed, and the one that points at you

hook.title: The Map Split in Two
hook.content: England both languages kept, and for the best reason in this course: the Angles were a Germanic tribe from Angeln, a small peninsula in Schleswig, and when they sailed west their name became England — the Angles' land — and their tongue became English. You are not studying a foreign cousin; English is a Germanic dialect that moved next door and borrowed a Roman wardrobe. Deutschland German built from deutsch: Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, 'of the (our) people', with the same þ→d hardening that made drei out of three and Bruder out of brother — while English borrowed the Dutch form of that very word as Dutch, pointed it at the Netherlands, and took Germany's own name from Latin Germani instead. Frankreich is the Franks' realm: reich is English rich wearing the k→ch badge (Buch/book, brechen/break), and the Franks were so famously the free men of Gaul that English borrowed their very name as the adjective frank. Spanien and Italien are simply Rome's names — Hispania and Italia — which both languages kept as Rome left them.

footnotes.title: The People-Word English Lost
footnotes.content: The root of deutsch, Proto-Germanic *þeudō, 'people', was Old English þēod. English let it die and kept the family only by borrowing: Dutch (from the Dutch form of *þiudiskaz) and Teutonic (from the Latinized form). German kept the native word and made a country of it — the people's land.

pattern.title: Countries in Frames
pattern.content: Three frames, and no article anywhere. 1. Dwell: Ich wohne in Deutschland — the bare country, exactly like German cities. 2. Move: Ich fahre nach Frankreich, Wir urlauben in Spanien — nach for travel toward a country, in for being inside it. 3. Originate: Er kommt aus England — aus for where someone is from. And the adjective that got away: Frankreich ist schön und reich — reich is the ordinary word 'rich', doing double duty inside the country name.
pattern.linguist_note: Country names are migration sediment. The Angles named England and, through it, the English language; the Franks named Francia — and, because in Frankish Gaul only the Franks were free, their name became the adjective frank 'free'; the Romans wrote Germani, origin uncertain, and English kept Rome's label. German answered all of it with one native compound: the people's land.

exercises.prompt: Five countries, no article — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: Spain is in the south, England in the north
matching_pairs.german: Spanien ist im Süden, England im Norden

matching_pairs.english: In June we vacation in Spain, in July in Italy
matching_pairs.german: Im Juni urlauben wir in Spanien, im Juli in Italien

exercises.target_answer: Ich wohne in Deutschland, Ich fahre nach Frankreich, Er kommt aus England, Wir urlauben in Spanien, Italien ist sehr schön, Spanien ist im Süden, England im Norden, Im Juni urlauben wir in Spanien, im Juli in Italien, Italien ist nicht fern, Spanien ist auf der Karte, Mein Hund ist braun, Frankreich ist im Westen, Die Fähre nach Italien
exercises.meaning: live in, travel to, come from, vacation in, is beautiful
exercises.explanation: Dwell in, move nach, come aus: the three prepositions do the whole grammar, and none of the five countries takes an article. urlauben is Urlaub made into a verb — German verbifies, English paraphrases.

exercises.prompt: deutsch hardened the old þ to d — *þiudiskaz, 'of the people'. Which pair wears the same TH→D badge?
exercises.meaning: deutsch is *þiudiskaz with the TH→D badge, like Bruder/brother
exercises.explanation: Bruder/brother is TH→D: same Proto-Germanic word, German hardened þ, English kept th. Tag/day runs the other way (D→T — German hardened d), and zehn/ten is T→S. Three badges, three directions, one family album.

exercises.prompt: English narrowed the old Germanic word for 'the people's tongue' ('deutsch' / 'Dietsch') to name the language of the Netherlands. What is that English word?
exercises.meaning: deutsch ↔ Dutch: one word, two neighbors
exercises.explanation: Deutsch and Dutch are the same word — *þiudiskaz, 'of the people'. English took the Dutch form duutsc, aimed it at the Netherlands, and named Germany with Latin Germani instead. deuce is French deux, 'two', and Dane is a different tribe entirely — false friends on both flanks.
wohnt is wohnen in slot 2 after Mein Freund takes slot 1 — the swap you have drilled all course. The bank's two other countries fit the same frame: Mein Freund wohnt in Spanien, in Deutschland.
reich is the ordinary adjective 'rich' — the k→ch twin of English rich (Buch/book) — doing double duty inside the country name: the realm of the Franks, who gave English the adjective frank.

summary.outcome: Say where you live, where you travel and where you are from — five country names, three prepositions, no articles.

use_example.german: Ich wohne in Deutschland — mein Bruder wohnt in England.
use_example.english: I live in Germany — my brother lives in England.

summary.takeaway: England is the Angles' land from Angeln; deutsch and Dutch are one word (*þiudiskaz, TH→D); reich is rich (k→ch); Frankreich is the Franks' realm; Spanien and Italien are Rome's own names.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the neighbors — and the two countries whose names insist on bringing their own article.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Länder I: Deutschland, Frankreich, England, Spanien, Italien (France is beautiful and rich):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Frankreich ist schön und reich" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Länder I: Deutschland, Frankreich, England, Spanien, Italien without relying on short-term echo.

deutschland.etymology_derivation: diutsch "of the people" + lant "land" — compound: land of the people. [wiktionary]

frankreich.etymology_derivation: Franke "Frank" + Reich "realm" — realm of the Franks. [wiktionary]

england.etymology_derivation: From Old English Engla land — land of the Angles. [wiktionary]

spanien.etymology_derivation: The same Latin name Hispania that English Spain descends from, via Old High German Spānia. [wiktionary]

italien.etymology_derivation: The same Latin name Italia as English Italy; shared proper name, no sound shift to fake. [wiktionary]

norden.context_translation: In the north it often rains.
norden.etymology_derivation: The compass noun from Nord, the twin of north; used with im for in the north. [wiktionary]

süden.context_phrase: Im Süden ist die Sonne stärker.
süden.context_translation: In the south the sun is stronger.
süden.etymology_derivation: From Middle Low German süden, ultimately Proto-Germanic *sunþanē — the old noun *sunþrą gave both English south and German Süd (th → d). [wiktionary]

westen.context_phrase: Die Sonne geht im Westen unter.
westen.context_translation: The sun sets in the west.
westen.etymology_derivation: The compass noun from West, the twin of west; used with im for in the west. [wiktionary]

braun.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *brūn — English brown is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

fern.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ferrai — the same word as English far (see der Fernseher, far-seer). [wiktionary]

karte.context_phrase: Ich brauche eine Karte für die U-Bahn.
karte.context_translation: I need a ticket for the underground.
karte.etymology_derivation: From Latin charta through Old French carte — the page compares English card: the same paper-word, borrowed in both languages. [wiktionary]

fähre.context_phrase: Die Fähre fährt über den Fluss.
fähre.context_translation: The ferry goes across the river.
fähre.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *farjo, the ferrying word of the same far-root as fahren — the page lists English ferry as cognate. [wiktionary]

rot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *raudaz; English red is the same root — English d ↔ German t. [wiktionary]

juni.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iūnius. [wiktionary]

juli.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iūlius. [wiktionary]

deutsch.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz, of the people, built on *þeudō, people; the very same word as English Dutch, with Latin theodiscus and Teutonic sharing the root. [wiktionary]

bruder.etymology_derivation: Medial th shifted to d; unstressed -er vocalizes to [ɐ].

wohnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wunāną, from the 'wish, love' root; no English cognate named on Wiktionary. [wiktionary]

freund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frijōndz, 'the loving one' — the exact twin of English friend. [wiktionary]

urlaub.context_phrase: Ich fahre im Urlaub nach Italien.
urlaub.context_translation: I go to Italy on vacation.
urlaub.etymology_derivation: Middle High German urloup 'permission to be away', kin to erlauben — cognate with English leave. [wiktionary]

stadt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *stadiz — the twin of stead (homestead, instead); final d devoiced to [t]. [wiktionary]

schön.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skauniz — the twin of archaic English sheen 'beautiful'. [wiktionary]

knoblauch.context_phrase: Ich gebe Knoblauch in die Soße.
knoblauch.context_translation: I add garlic to the sauce.
knoblauch.etymology_derivation: Old High German chlobalouh, literally clove leek; Knob- comes from klieben, meaning to cleave, and Lauch is cognate with English leek, which garlic preserves in its own spear-leek compound. [wiktionary]

bach.etymology_derivation: From Old High German bah, from Proto-West Germanic *baki. Northern English beck is the living cognate, keeping the k where German shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
